data.title: Middle East Eye: Netanyahu sought private talks with Palestinian party leader despite public attacks
data.author: Oscar Rickett
data.summary:
Netanyahu sought private talks with Palestinian party leader despite public attacks
The leader of the United Arab List, Mansour Abbas, said on Wednesday that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had held private talks with him through a close associate, despite publicly branding Palestinian parties "terror supporters who hate Israel".
"He was interested in our position on the law barring an indicted lawmaker from serving as prime minister, and whether we really intended to enter a coalition and replace Netanyahu's government," Abbas told Kan public radio.
"When it serves his interests, Arab citizens suddenly become legitimate, he becomes 'Abu Yair', and Mansour Abbas becomes a worthy partner in his eyes."
The Palestinian-led United Arab List (Ra'am) and the Joint List won a record 19 seats combined, following a surge in turnout among Palestinian voters in Israel, giving them the balance of power.
In a speech to parliament on Tuesday evening, Netanyahu said the United Arab List and the Joint List were seeking to end Israel’s existence, adding that the two parties disagreed only on "what kind of state will arise on its ruins".

Egyptian naval warships had also moved towards the southern Red Sea, near the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, the source added.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Revealed: West Bank petrol station chain faces $325m claim in PA fuel-smuggling probe
data.author: Fleur Hargreaves
data.summary:
Revealed: West Bank petrol station chain faces $325m claim in PA fuel-smuggling probe
A petrol station chain owned by one of the West Bank’s wealthiest businessmen is facing accusations of alleged fuel smuggling, financial misconduct and tax evasion totalling more than 1bn shekels ($325m), according to a leaked report seen by Middle East Eye.
The investigation, which has unfolded against a backdrop of worsening fuel shortages in the occupied Palestinian territory, has led to the arrest and weeks-long detention of Tarek al-Natsheh, the chairman of Al-Huda Group, as well as raids by security forces on his company’s offices and the confiscation of computers and financial records.
Lawyers for Natsheh, who is accused in the report of profiting from smuggling activities, say he denies wrongdoing and stands ready to pay any taxes he may legally owe.
They say the company and Natsheh are cooperating with legal proceedings, but have criticised his detention, commenting that “personal freedom should not be used as a means of pressure to accept figures whose accuracy has not been established”.
MEE sent a detailed list of questions and a request for comment to Malek al-Awri, legal adviser for the defence team, ahead of publication of this article. Awri referred MEE to a previous statement he had given to the Palestinian Watan newspaper last month.

data.author: Oscar Rickett

Netanyahu accused of giving 'hate-filled speech' in Israeli parliament
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was accused of giving a "hate-filled speech" against the Palestinian-led parties in the newly elected parliament on Tuesday.
On Tuesday, two weeks after Netanyahu's far-right bloc lost the elections following an historic voter turnout from Palestinian citizens of Israel, the parliament was sworn in in Jerusalem, with an unprecedented 19 members from the Palestinian-led Joint List alliance and Ra'am party.
Marking the ceremonial day, Netanyahu initially told the new Knesset members that Israel was facing "great threats" from Iran's nuclear programme, stating that "the only way to remove this existential threat permanently is by toppling the regime of the ayatollahs".
However, after boasting about Israeli military achievements in the occupied Palestinian territories, Syria, Lebanon and Iran, Netanyahu began lashing out at the Palestinian-led parties.
The Israeli premier said that Israel must "set aside every other consideration and form a national unity government" with his main challenger Gadi Eisenkot.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Rubio says US sees 'two or three very qualified people' for top UN job
data.author: Oscar Rickett
data.summary:
Rubio says US sees 'two or three very qualified people' for top UN job
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said that the US believes there are "two or three very qualified people" for the job of United Nations secretary general, which will shortly be vacated by Antonio Guterres.
In remarks reported by PassBlue, which covers the UN, Rubio said that if he revealed who Washington's preferred candidate was, "it would doom them to lose".
"There's a couple really good candidates, people that we like, two or three, and the process will work itself out," Rubio said. "And I think we've expressed our views, but that - it's an ongoing process."
US President Donald Trump's administration favours Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh for the job, according to multiple diplomatic sources who have spoken with Middle East Eye.
Her candidacy has been the subject of much controversy surrounding Abu Dhabi's support for the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, which has been found by the UN and US to have committed genocide in Darfur.
"At some point the world will make a decision on who they want, and we have our opinions," Rubio said.
"I talked about that with [French] President [Emmanuel] Macron just a moment ago, but I think we're just going to keep working it the way we are right now because other countries get a vote here as well."
France is also believed to be backing Nusseibeh. "I hope France is aligned with us on the need to reform the United Nations," Rubio said. "The whole system is in need of reform."

SEC RUBIO: If I told you who the U.S. – if I told you who the U.S. wanted it, it would doom them to lose.

SEC RUBIO: No, there’s a couple…

data.title: Middle East Eye: Russian negotiator rejects territorial swaps with Ukraine as Abu Dhabi talks end
data.author: Oscar Rickett
data.summary:
Russian negotiator rejects territorial swaps with Ukraine as Abu Dhabi talks end
After two days of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi, Russia's chief negotiator said there was no possibility of exchanging territory with Ukraine as part of any peace deal, Russia's Tass news agency reported on Wednesday.
Vladimir Medinsky and Ukrainian negotiators had earlier reported some progress in the talks, which ended on Wednesday. But US mediators said there was a lack of trust between the warring sides and differences remained on a number of issues, including territory.
Medinsky was also cited as saying that if what he called a fair security system for Europe could be created, it would help ensure peace on the continent for decades, and possibly centuries, to come.
He added that Russia's buffer zone along its border with Ukraine was already substantial and would keep expanding, according to the Interfax news agency, as cited by Reuters.

data.author: Oscar Rickett

Saudi air defences intercept Houthi cruise missiles launched toward Riyadh
Saudi air defences intercepted Houthi missiles launched toward the Riyadh region for the second consecutive day on Wednesday, according to the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Yemeni movement.
The coalition said the Iran-aligned Houthis launched three cruise missiles that were destroyed.
The armed group, which controls most of the populous parts of Yemen, has intensified attacks on Saudi Arabia's capital in recent days. A Houthi attack on Sunday damaged an Aramco administrative building in Riyadh's financial hub.
On Tuesday, Saudi air defences intercepted a ballistic missile and a cruise missile launched towards Riyadh, the coalition said.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Retrial of Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah suspended
data.author: Oscar Rickett
data.summary:
Retrial of Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah suspended
An Egyptian court on Wednesday adjourned the retrial of Mada Masr editor-in-chief Lina Attalah until 18 November to consider a defence request for the judge’s removal, the independent news outlet said.
Attalah faces charges of publishing false news and operating a website without a licence in a case in which she was sentenced to a year in prison in her absence in 2024.
Mada Masr’s lawyer, Hassan al-Azhari, said the defence would submit its grounds for seeking the judge’s removal ahead of the next hearing, arguing that he had “already formed a view against the defendant”.
The presiding judge, Mohamed Mubarak, also issued a ruling on 27 October in a separate case fining Attalah three million Egyptian pounds (about $56,000) and ordering Mada Masr’s closure.
The proceedings come amid a wider crackdown on independent media, including the detention in September of all six journalists working for fact-checking outlet Matsadaash.

Gaza has suffered an ecocide as well as a genocide, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said on Wednesday during his opening address at the Cop31 climate conference, which is being held in Antalya.
“As I also emphasised in my address to the UN General Assembly, Gaza has suffered not only genocide but also ecocide,” Erdogan said of the Palestinian enclave, which has been subject to an Israeli onslaught since October 2023.
“Centuries-old olive trees have been cut down, the soil and water have been contaminated, and cities have been reduced to enormous piles of rubble.”
Erdogan said heavy rainfall and flooding had compounded the humanitarian suffering in Gaza, leaving tens of thousands of tents and shelters submerged.
“Hundreds of thousands of our brothers and sisters in Gaza, with no roof under which to take shelter, especially innocent children trembling with cold, are struggling to survive amid the floodwaters in these winter conditions, often without their mothers or fathers,” he said.
The Turkish president called for humanitarian aid to be allowed into Gaza immediately and for an end to the policy of isolation.
Climate change is a deep existential crisis
Turning to the broader climate crisis, Erdogan described climate change as “one of the deepest existential crises” in humanity’s history.
“As humanity, our home has only one roof, and that is the sky. As humanity, our home has only one garden, and that is the Earth," he said.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Yemeni government forces report hundreds of strikes against Houthis
data.author: Fleur Hargreaves
data.summary:
Yemeni government forces report hundreds of strikes against Houthis
The Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces said on Wednesday that they have carried out hundreds of strikes targeting the Houthis.
Majed Abdullah al-Nuzaili, a spokesperson for Yemen’s government forces, said in a post on X that the army carried out 773 field artillery bombings, 44 drone strikes, 37 rocket attacks and 23 air strikes, which killed and wounded 138 Houthi fighters and damaged 86 heavy weapons and military vehicles.
Nuzaili added that operations in al-Jawf, Marib, al-Bayda, Taiz and the southern sectors against the Houthis continue.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Iran's top negotiator says Tehran has no desire for war to continue
data.author: Fleur Hargreaves
data.summary:
Iran's top negotiator says Tehran has no desire for war to continue
Iran's parliament speaker and head of its negotiating team, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said in an interview with Al Jazeera on Wednesday that Tehran has no desire to continue the war with the US, but the ball is in Washington's court for peace talks.
Ghalibaf said that Iran provided the US with a clear and transparent response outlining its demands, but the Trump administration has not yet reponded.
An agreement with Washington is possible, he added, provided it adheres to what was previously agreed upon and refrains from actions that undermine trust and excessive demands.
He said that Iran is determined to move beyond the state of “no war, no peace” through negotiations or sustainable deterrence, and accused Washington of imposing a siege on the country by blocking access to food and hindering trade and healthcare services.
However, he said that the Strait of Hormuz will not return to its pre-war status, adding that its future would be determined within a seven-point framework proposed by Tehran.
Finally, Ghalibaf told Al Jazeera that the US visited Moscow and asked President Vladimir Putin to speak with Iran to facilitate direct negotiations.

data.author: Fleur Hargreaves
data.summary:
WHO reports almost 12,000 casualties in renewed Yemen fighting
The World Health Organisation (WHO) warned on Wednesday that casualties from the fighting in Yemen have risen sharply to 11,755 - including 2,098 killed and 9,657 wounded - as of 8 November.
The United Nations agency added that over 2,000 casualties were recorded in just nine days, with Marib and Lahj among the worst affected governorates, and more than 320,000 people have been displaced since 1 August, including nearly 16,000 in the past week.
The WHO said strikes have also hit health facilities and ambulances, and warned that critical fuel shortages are disrupting emergency medical services in Taiz.

Security chief Mohsen Rezaei warns Tehran will reciprocate against any US attack emanating from Europe
Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei attends consultations with members of the Mecca Joint Defence in Tehran, Iran, on 26 October 2026 (Iranian Presidency via Zuma Press)

Iran has no intention of surrendering its enriched nuclear material, which it wants to use to build nuclear-powered submarines, security chief Mohsen Rezaei said on Wednesday, in an apparent rejection of US demands to give up the material for a political settlement.
In an interview with Al Mayadeen TV network, Rezaei said Iran will not allow a “single speck” of enriched uranium to leave the country.
"We need the enriched material to design ships and submarines that work on nuclear energy," Rezaei said, adding that Tehran has informed Moscow that its enriched nuclear material will remain in the country and "we will use it ourselves".
Rezaei’s remarks come a day after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called Iran’s terms for a political settlement “absurd” and stressed that the Trump administration believes its maritime blockade against Iran gives them the upper hand in negotiations.
Rezaei, who has become more prominent in the media in recent months for explaining Iran’s terms, struck a defiant tone in his interview.
“If American aircraft take off from an American military base, even one located in a European country or some other distant region, to bomb Iran, we will strike those bases as well," Rezaei said.
He also said that Iran's response to renewed US attacks would "target America's more distant military installations - including the ones we have not yet attacked", without specifying details.
"We may even strike certain islands that they assume are beyond the reach of our missiles," he added.
